hints: Trace where Purkyne tissue sits in the sequence: it comes after the AV node and bundle of His and carries impulses down into the ventricles, so ask yourself which chamber contracts because of it on the right side.

Remember that structures earlier in the pathway (SAN for starting impulses, AVN for delay, atria for first contraction) work before Purkyne tissue, so damage to right-side Purkyne will only slow the response downstream of that point.
walkthrough:
**Recall the normal conduction pathway**

Think of the heartbeat as a wave travelling in order. It starts at the sinoatrial node, spreads over the atria so they contract, then pauses briefly at the atrioventricular node.

Then it goes: AVN to bundle of His to Purkyne tissue to ventricle muscle, causing the ventricles to contract from the apex upwards.

**Locate the damage**

Here only the Purkyne tissue to the right side is slowed. That is very late and very local in the pathway.

It cannot change what already happened upstream at the SAN, the atria, or the AVN.

**Predict the downstream effect**

The left Purkyne tissue is still normal, so the left ventricle gets its signal on time. The right Purkyne tissue is slow, so the right ventricle gets its signal late.

Result: the right ventricle muscle contracts slightly more slowly, or out of sync, compared with the left ventricle. That matches option B.

options.A: The AVN delay happens before impulses reach Purkyne tissue, so damage downstream in right Purkyne cannot cause the AVN to delay impulses.
options.B: Purkyne tissue triggers ventricular contraction, so slower transmission on the right means the right ventricle contracts slightly later than the normal left ventricle.
options.C: Atrial contraction is triggered by the SAN before the AVN and Purkyne tissue are involved, so right atrial contraction would be unaffected.
options.D: The SAN is the pacemaker upstream that starts all impulses, so its rate of firing is not reduced by slower conduction much later in right Purkyne tissue.
